It opened on 25 November 2020{{cite web |title=Opening of the 53rd Parliament |url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/visit-and-learn/parliament-in-election-year/opening-of-the-53rd-parliament/ |website=www.parliament.nz |publisher=New Zealand Parliament |access-date=25 November 2020 |language=en-NZ |archive-date=6 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201106024642/https://www.parliament.nz/en/visit-and-learn/parliament-in-election-year/opening-of-the-53rd-parliament |url-status=dead }} following the [[2020 New Zealand general election|17 October 2020 general election]], and dissolved on 8 September 2023 to trigger the [[2023 New Zealand general election|next election]]. It consisted of 120 [[Member of parliament|members of Parliament]] (MPs){{cite web |url= https://www.parliament.nz/en/visit-and-learn/how-parliament-works/our-system-of-government/ |title=Our system of government |publisher=[[New Zealand Parliament]] |access-date=28 January 2020}} with five [[Political parties in New Zealand|parties]] represented: the [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]] and [[Green Party of New Zealand|Green]] parties, in [[Executive (government)|government]], and the [[New Zealand National Party|National]], [[Māori Party|Māori]] and [[ACT New Zealand|ACT]] parties, in [[Parliamentary opposition|opposition]]. The [[Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand|Sixth Labour Government]] held a majority in this Parliament. [[Jacinda Ardern]] continued as [[Prime minister of New Zealand|prime minister]] until her resignation on 25 January 2023; she was succeeded by [[Chris Hipkins]]. The Parliament was elected using a [[mixed-member proportional representation]] (MMP) voting system. MPs represented 72 geographical electorates: 16 in the [[South Island]], 49 in the [[North Island]] and 7 [[Māori electorates]]. This was an increase of one electorate seat from the previous election, as a result of population growth in the North Island. The remaining MPs were elected from [[Party lists in the 2020 New Zealand general election|party lists]] using the [[Webster/Sainte-Laguë method]] to realise proportionality.{{cite web |title=MMP maths: How party vote percentages become seats in parliament |url=https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/14-09-2017/mmp-maths-how-party-vote-percentages-become-seats-in-parliament/ |work=[[The Spinoff]] |first=Simon |last=Wilson |access-date=8 September 2020 |date=14 September 2017}} == Background == === Electorate changes === To achieve proportionality across electorates, there were a number of changes required to electorates based on population data determined through the [[2018 New Zealand census|2018 census]] and projected population growth.{{cite web |title=Working out how many September 2020}} The 2020 election resulted in a majority for the [[Labour Party (New Zealand)|Labour Party]], winning 65 seats, allowing them to continue the [[Sixth Labour Government]] unrestricted. Their coalition partner from the 52nd Parliament, [[New Zealand First]], did not receive enough votes to pass the five percent threshold or win in an [[New Zealand electorates|electorate]], kicking them out of Parliament. [[Confidence and supply]] partner the [[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Green Party]] received 10 seats, up two, becoming the first minor party ever to increase their share of the vote following their being in government. In the opposition, the [[National Party (New Zealand)|National Party]] lost 23 seats, giving them a total of 33, and [[ACT New Zealand]] went from one seat to ten. The [[Māori Party]] won the [[Waiariki (New Zealand electorate)|Waiariki]] electorate and gained an additional list seat after losing representation in the 2017 general election.{{cite web|title=New Zealand Election Results|url=https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/|access-date=27 November 2020|website=ElectionResults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/|publisher=Electoral Commission}} === Government formation === Labour achieved a majority in the 2020 election, allowing them to form a government without any [[coalition]] agreements having to be made. However, Prime Minister [[Jacinda Ardern]] entered talks with the Green Party about "potential areas of co-operation" in the formation of the new government.{{cite news |title=Labour kicks off Government forming talks with the Greens in Jacinda Ardern's Beehive office |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/labour-kicks-off-government-forming-talks-with-the-greens-in-jacinda-arderns-beehive-office/TIATRS37XGVRRU2VW2Y4CFCWCY/ |access-date=25 October 2020 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=21 October 2020}} After two weeks of discussions, the Green Party reached an agreement with Labour on 31 October to become part of the next Government, with co-leaders [[James Shaw (New Zealand politician)|James Shaw]] and [[Marama Davidson]] receiving ministerial positions outside of cabinet. Shaw remained [[Minister for Climate Change (New Zealand)|Minister for Climate Change]] and become Associate Minister for the Environment, while Davidson became [[Minister for the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence]] and Associate Minister of Housing.{{cite news|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300146558/election-2020-green-party-votes-to-be-part-of-next-government-with-labour|title=Election 2020: Green Party votes to be part of next Government with Labour|first1=Thomas|last1=Coughlan|first2=Henry|last2=Cooke|date=31 October 2020|access-date=1 November 2020}} The new government was sworn in on 6 November 2020. Some ministerial positions changed in July 2021. Ardern was succeeded as prime minister by [[Chris Hipkins]] on 25 January 2023, following her resignation. ==Parliamentary term== The writ for the 2020 election was returned on 20 November 2020{{cite tweet|user=ElectoralCommNZ|number=1329633612157825025|date=20 November 2020|title=The Electoral Commission has returned the writ for the 2020 General Election following the completion of the recounts in Te Tai Hauāuru and Tāmaki Makaurau. The return of the writ marks the end of the election process. More information:}} after being delayed from its original set date of 12 November due to election recounts. Under section 19 of [[Constitution Act 1986]], Parliament must meet no later than six weeks after this date; on 6 November 2020, following the new government's first Cabinet meeting, Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern confirmed that the Commission Opening and State Opening of Parliament would take place on 25 and 26 November 2020, respectively. The 53rd Parliament is the first parliament since the [[44th New Zealand Parliament]] (and the introduction of an MMP electoral system) to have a single party hold an outright majority of seats. The Labour Party currently holds 64 seats, 3 more than the required 61 seats needed for a majority.{{cite news |title=New Zealand election: Jacinda Ardern's Labour Party scores landslide win |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-54519628 |access-date=3 November 2020 |work=[[BBC News]] |date=17 October 2020}} === Timeline === *1 November 2020 – The [[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Green Party]] enter into a "cooperation agreement" with [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]] *6 November 2020 – **[[Jacinda Ardern]] is sworn in for a second term as prime minister. legislation === {{See also|List of acts of the 53rd New Zealand Parliament}} On 1 March 2021, the [[Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021]] received royal assent after being introduced by [[Nanaia Mahuta]] on 9 February. This Act eliminates mechanisms for holding public [[referendum]]s on the establishment of [[Māori wards and constituencies]] on local bodies, which allowed the public to veto a council's decision to introduce a Māori ward.{{cite news |last1=Scotcher |first1=Katie |title=Māori wards amendment bill passes final reading in Parliament |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/437105/maori-wards-amendment-bill-passes-final-reading-in-parliament |access-date=23 March 2021 |work=[[Radio NZ]] |date=24 February 2021}} On 30 September 2021, the [[Counter-Terrorism Legislation Act 2021]] passed its third reading. This Act criminalised the planning of terror attacks and expanded Police powers to conduct warrantless searches. It was supported by the Labour and National parties but was opposed by the Green, ACT and Māori parties.{{cite news |last1=Manch |first1=Thomas |title=Parliament passes counter-terrorism laws, criminalising terror planning and expanding warrantless search powers |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/126530458/parliament-passes-counterterrorism-laws-criminalising-terror-planning-and-expanding-warrantless-search-powers |access-date=1 October 2021 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=30 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210930005143/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/126530458/parliament-passes-counterterrorism-laws-criminalising-terror-planning-and-expanding-warrantless-search-powers |archive-date=30 September 2021|url-status=live}} On 24 November 2021, the [[COVID-19 Response (Vaccinations) Legislation Act 2021]] passed its third reading. This Act allows businesses to dismiss employees who refuse to take COVID-19 vaccines.{{cite news |title=Mandate legislation pushed through Parliament amid fierce opposition |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/456455/mandate-legislation-pushed-through-parliament-amid-fierce-opposition |access-date=24 November 2021 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=24 November 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211124104338/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/456455/mandate-legislation-pushed-through-parliament-amid-fierce-opposition |archive-date=24 November 2021|url-status=live}} On 15 December 2021, the [[Resource Management (Enabling Housing Supply and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2021]] passed its third and final reading with the support of all parties except ACT. The Act seeks to address the national housing shortage by easing the process for building houses in major cities.{{cite news |title=Resource Management Act amendment passes final reading |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/resource-management-act-amendment-passes-final-reading/TJEKPQPBAUZ7S4TV65XMRAIZ5E/ |access-date=15 December 2021 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=14 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211214121608/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/resource-management-act-amendment-passes-final-reading/TJEKPQPBAUZ7S4TV65XMRAIZ5E/ |archive-date=14 December 2021|url-status=live}}{{cite news |title=Resource Management Act amendment passes final reading |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/457924/resource-management-act-amendment-passes-final-reading |access-date=15 December 2021 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=14 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211214133820/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/457924/resource-management-act-amendment-passes-final-reading |archive-date=14 December 2021|url-status=live}} On 15 February 2022, the [[Conversion Practices Prohibition Legislation Act 2022]] passed its third reading, becoming law with broad cross-party support. The Act banned [[conversion therapy]] in New Zealand.{{Cite news|date=15 February 2022|title=Politicians react as bill to ban conversion therapy passes|url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/461599/politicians-react-as-bill-to-ban-conversion-therapy-passes|access-date=21 February 2022|work=[[Radio New Zealand]]|language=en-nz|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220218050733/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/461599/politicians-react-as-bill-to-ban-conversion-therapy-passes|archive-date=18 February 2022|url-status=live}} On 9 March 2022, Parliament unanimously passed the [[Russia Sanctions Act 2022]], which established a sanctions-implementation regime targeting Russia in response to the [[Russian invasion of Ukraine]].{{cite news |title=Parliament unanimously passes Russia Sanctions Bill |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/463022/parliament-unanimously-passes-russia-sanctions-bill |access-date=11 March 2022 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=9 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220309155948/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/463022/parliament-unanimously-passes-russia-sanctions-bill |archive-date=9 March 2022|url-status=live}}{{cite news |title=Russia invasion of Ukraine: Parliament passes Russia Sanctions Act unanimously |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/russia-invasion-of-ukraine-parliament-passes-russia-sanctions-act-unanimously/SGMIYENM6FUCGOXRWQYH2FILBM/ |access-date=11 March 2022 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=9 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220309100539/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/russia-invasion-of-ukraine-parliament-passes-russia-sanctions-act-unanimously/SGMIYENM6FUCGOXRWQYH2FILBM/ |archive-date=9 March 2022|url-status=live}} On 18 March 2022, the [[Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion (Safe Areas) Amendment Act 2022]] received royal assent. The Bill creates safe spaces of about 150 metres around abortion providers and also bans obstructing, filming, dissuading or protesting against individuals seeking abortion services in those zones.{{cite news |last1=O'Dwyer |first1=Ellen |title='Safe areas' abortion law passes with large majority in Parliament |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/128080358/safe-areas-abortion-law-passes-with-large-majority-in-parliament |access-date=21 March 2022 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=16 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220316091629/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/128080358/safe-areas-abortion-law-passes-with-large-majority-in-parliament |archive-date=16 March 2022}} On 7 June 2022, the Government's [[Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022]] passed its third reading. The Bill replaced the country's existing [[district health board]]s with a new Crown agency called [[Health New Zealand]] and established as separate [[Māori Health Authority]]. The Health Futures Act also established a new [[Public Health Agency (New Zealand)|Public Health Agency]] within the [[Ministry of Health (New Zealand)|Ministry of Health]] while strengthening the Ministry's stewardship role.{{cite news |title=New Health System Act passes third reading in Parliament |url=https://www.1news.co.nz/2022/06/08/new-health-system-act-passes-third-reading-in-parliament/ |access-date=10 June 2022 |work=[[1News]] |publisher=[[TVNZ]] |date=8 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220607184346/https://www.1news.co.nz/2022/06/08/new-health-system-act-passes-third-reading-in-parliament/ |archive-date=7 June 2022|url-status=live}} On 9 August 2022, the Government's [[Three Strikes Legislation Repeal Act 2022]] passed its third reading, repealing the [[Sentencing and Parole Reform Act 2010]]. The Three Strikes Legislation Repeal Act removed the [[three strikes law]] from New Zealand legislation. While the bill was supported by the Labour, Green, and Māori parties, it was opposed by the National and ACT parties.{{cite news |last1=Huang |first1=Christina |title=Parliament votes to scrap three strikes law |url=https://www.1news.co.nz/2022/08/09/parliament-votes-to-scrap-three-strikes-law/ |access-date=10 August 2022 |work=[[1News]] |publisher=[[TVNZ]] |date=9 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220810025038/https://www.1news.co.nz/2022/08/09/parliament-votes-to-scrap-three-strikes-law/ |archive-date=10 August 2022}}{{cite news |last1=Neilson |first1=Michael |title=Three strikes law gone: Labour fulfils 2017 campaign promise, Nats and Act rail against move |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/three-strikes-law-gone-labour-fulfils-2017-campaign-promise-nats-and-act-rail-against-move/YOI73MBFQOCURPHDLJXJNH4E3U/ |access-date=10 August 2022 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=9 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220809140551/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/three-strikes-law-gone-labour-fulfils-2017-campaign-promise-nats-and-act-rail-against-move/YOI73MBFQOCURPHDLJXJNH4E3U/ |archive-date=9 August 2022}} On 13 December, the [[Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022]] passed its third reading and became law. The bill banned tobacco from being sold to anyone born after 1 January 2009, limited the number of retailers allowed to sell tobacco, and lowered the nicotine content in tobacco products.{{cite news |last1=McClure |first1=Tess |title=New Zealand passes world-first tobacco law to ban smoking for next generation |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/dec/13/new-zealand-passes-world-first-tobacco-law-to-ban-smoking-by-2025 |access-date=29 November 2023 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=13 December 2022}} On 16 August 2023, the Water Services Entities Amendment Act 2023 passed its third reading.
